analysis.one_liner: Overhauls federal chemical safety law to require companies to prove their chemicals are safe before selling them.
analysis.headline: The Safe Chemicals Act, with 29 Senate cosponsors, was referred to the Environment and Public Works Committee in April 2013 and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Safe Chemicals Act would have rewritten the nation's main chemical safety law, the Toxic Substances Control Act. Today, chemicals can stay on the market unless the government proves they are dangerous; this bill would have flipped that, making companies prove their chemicals are safe before selling them. It would have required safety reviews of all chemicals in commerce, immediately restricted asbestos, let states keep stricter rules, and given the public and workers more access to information about chemical hazards. The bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people, especially children, pregnant women, workers who handle chemicals, and communities with heavy chemical exposure. The bill would have required companies to prove their chemicals are safe before selling them, given the EPA power and deadlines to review and restrict the most dangerous substances, immediately restricted asbestos, and expanded the public's and workers' right to know about chemical hazards. It also preserved states' ability to set tougher rules and made it easier for citizens to sue violators.

how_it_helps.text: Requires manufacturers to prove their chemicals meet a health-based safety standard before they can be sold, reversing the current practice in which chemicals stay on the market until regulators prove harm.
Directs the EPA to review all chemicals in commerce, beginning with the most hazardous and widely encountered, and to restrict substances of very high concern within 18 months of designation.
Designates asbestos as a substance of very high concern and requires immediate restrictions to reduce exposure to the maximum extent practicable.
Guarantees public and worker access to information on chemical hazards and uses, and requires disclosure when hazardous chemicals are found in products for children 14 and younger.
Preserves states' rights to set stricter chemical rules than the federal government and expands citizens' ability to sue and petition for enforcement.

analysis.who_pays: Chemical manufacturers and processors, who would bear the cost of testing every substance, submitting detailed safety information, and restricting or withdrawing chemicals that cannot be shown safe—costs that could be passed to consumers in product prices.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs for chemical manufacturers and processors would be significant: they must fund testing, submit minimum information sets, and can face testing orders, and some costs would likely be passed to consumers in prices.

The bill requires the EPA to complete safety determinations for Priority Class 1 substances within five years and to work through the entire inventory in batches, a large administrative undertaking whose deadlines could outpace the agency's scientific and staffing capacity.
Determinations that a manufacturer failed to prove safety are shielded from judicial review, reducing a procedural check on EPA decisions that industry groups consider overbroad.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits—safety proof for thousands of untested chemicals, protection for children and exposed communities, the right to know what is in products—appear large, and the bill placed the burden of proof on industry rather than regulators. The costs are real but ordinary: compliance testing, reformulation, and paperwork for chemical makers, likely passed partly into prices, plus implementation costs for EPA. The main design question is pace and capacity—the law demanded safety determinations on tens of thousands of substances on tight deadlines, which could have overwhelmed the agency. Weighed against decades of unassessed exposure, the trade appears favorable to the public; what killed it was not a fair vote but the absence of one.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee in April 2013, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: S. 696 was introduced on April 10, 2013 and read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works, its only recorded action.
It carried 28 cosponsors (26 Democrats and 2 independents) in addition to sponsor Frank Lautenberg.
No further action—no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote—is recorded for the remainder of the 113th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Chemical manufacturers are better off: they avoid the burden of proving their products safe, and untested chemicals remain on the market.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Chemical manufacturers; the status quo held

for.name: Sen. Frank Lautenberg
for.role: U.S. Senator from New Jersey, bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and championed the overhaul of the Toxic Substances Control Act; he died in June 2013.

for.name: 28 Senate cosponsors
for.role: 26 Democrats and 2 independents in the Senate

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.role: Senate committee with jurisdiction over toxic substances law
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never reported it out, held no recorded markup, and took no further action on it.

against.name: Chemical industry (American Chemistry Council and allied manufacturers)
against.role: Industry trade groups and chemical manufacturers
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill's burden-of-proof and safety-standard provisions as overbroad and pushed instead for a more industry-favorable rewrite, which Congress ultimately enacted in 2016.

sides.party_line_note: All 29 supporters (sponsor plus cosponsors) were Democrats or independents; no Republican cosponsor is listed in the record.

industries.note: They would bear the burden of proving each chemical safe before selling it, supply health and safety data, and face restrictions, bans, and higher penalties for violations. Costs of testing and reformulation would fall on them and partly on consumers.

industries.industry: Testing, toxicology, and green chemistry firms
industries.note: The bill creates a permanent market for safety testing, alternative test methods, and the development of safer chemical alternatives, supported by federal grants and new research centers.
